claims.text: Conventionally cast or solidified refractory high-entropy alloys can have a homogeneous, coarse-grained microstructure with high strength but limited ductility and nonuniform deformation.
Controlled thermal aging at moderate temperatures can induce uniformly distributed nanoscale ductile precipitates in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The induced nanoscale ductile precipitates will be located particularly at grain boundaries within the high-strength matrix.
The nanoscale ductile precipitates will act as dislocation sinks.
The nanoscale ductile precipitates will serve as nucleation sites for localized deformation modes.
The precipitate-mediated deformation processes will promote distributed plastic flow.
The precipitate-mediated deformation processes will delay crack propagation.
Controlled aging will leave the high-strength matrix largely intact.
The thermally aged alloy will have greater tensile ductility than the untreated alloy.
The thermally aged alloy will deform more uniformly than the untreated alloy.
Thermal aging will leave yield strength essentially unchanged relative to the untreated alloy.
Thermal aging will leave impact-induced energy release essentially unchanged relative to the untreated alloy.
The proposed benefits should persist under both quasi-static and dynamic impact loading relevant to energetic structural applications.
Excessive precipitate coarsening or deleterious phase formation may negate the expected benefits.
Significant changes in aging conditions or alloy composition may negate the expected benefits.
